title: Being Julia
full_review:
English writer W. Somerset Maugham, best remembered today for his novels like "Of Human Bondage" and "The Razor's Edge," was also a canny playwright, and his plays -- occasionally revived in England -- can still come across with wit and brilliance.

More's the pity then that "Being Julia" (Sony Classics), an adaptation of his 1937 novel, "Theatre," first dramatized by Guy Bolton (it played in New York in 1941), is so oddly lacking in drama, even though it's been adapted by distinguished playwright Ronald Harwood and directed by the esteemed Istvan Szabo.

Perhaps it's having a Hungarian director and a big American star, Annette Bening -- distinguished artists though they are -- that ultimately detracts from the film's success. For the record, "Theatre" was filmed at least twice before: There was a 1978 Russian version and a 1962 French-German co-production, with Lilli Palmer and Charles Boyer, known as "Adorable Julia."

Here we have Bening as Julia Lambert, a larger-than-life English stage actress who is weary of performing in a long-running play, and is hoping for some excitement and novelty in her life. She begs her producer-husband Michael Gosselyn (Jeremy Irons) to close the play, but he demurs.

Michael introduces her to a young American fan, Tom Fennel (Shaun Evans), whom he's hired to do the accounting. The aging Julia's boredom at the prospect of spending time with him quickly turns to keen interest, and she seems blind to the opportunistic side of Tom. Before long, they embark on a full-out affair. (Julia's extramarital dalliances are far from admirable, it goes without saying, but the setup is as artificial as one of the drawing room comedies of the period in which Julia appears.)

Though she's old enough to be his mother, Tom makes her feel young again. Julia does, in fact, have a son, Roger (Tom Sturridge, in a likable portrayal), who's tolerant of his mother's foibles. At one point, Tom and Roger go out on the town looking to "meet girls," which is Julia's first clue that the relationship may be in jeopardy.

Tom's interest in her indeed begins to wane, when he falls under the spell of an aspiring and ambitious young actress named Avice Crichton (Lucy Punch). Aware of Tom's new infatuation, Julia agrees to facilitate Avice's audition for her new play. Matters are further complicated when Michael falls for the new actress.
Szabo is no stranger to period drama, having succeeded brilliantly with films like "Mephisto" and "Sunshine." But films about theater are, as a rule, difficult to pull off. Scenes of "great acting" on a proscenium stage often seem insufferably artificial when viewed through a camera's lens, and scenes of a rapt or wildly applauding audience often look contrived. Those pitfalls are not entirely avoided here.

Bening is very much the center of the action, and good actress though she is, she is not quite in her element as the grand actress, given to acting offstage as much as on. (One of the film's themes is theater as metaphor for role playing.) Her English accent is accomplished, and some of her on- and offstage moments show the requisite hauteur, but lovely period costuming notwithstanding, she seems not to inhabit the period and her performance rings strangely false. Her final scenery-chewing theatrical triumph is reasonably entertaining, but any number of English actresses might have been preferable overall.

Evans is absolutely wrong as her young lover. His American accent is fine (he's actually English, as was his character in the novel) but the line readings are totally contemporary, not at all the right type for an earnest young American of that period. Don't casting agents watch old movies to get a proper sense of style?

Michael Gambon is his usual scene-stealing self as Julia's late mentor who pops up periodically to give her no-nonsense advice. The movie also features Juliet Stevenson as her devoted assistant; Miriam Margolyes as Michael's pesky producing partner, whose infatuation with Julia masks lesbian attraction; Rosemary Harris and Rita Tushingham as Julia's mother and aunt, respectively; and Leigh Lawson and Bruce Greenwood, the latter another suitor of Julia's who ultimately reveals he's gay.
Motivations are not always clear. Why, for example, does Julia help her rival get a part in her play? Is it only to keep Tom? Or to ultimately humiliate Avice, as she does? (If so, the revenge motivation is less than praiseworthy.) And are we meant to think Avice is a bad actress? She certainly seems so, yet we're to believe everyone's wowed by her.

Theater lovers will enjoy this glossy film more than most, but there's undeniably something missing. The photography by Lajos Koltai is stunning, and the production design by Luciana Arrighi is appropriately luscious.

Because of a few instances of crude language, casual depiction of extramarital sex and an instance of rear nudity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
